subject: ela
intro: Narrative writing tells a story. A strong narrative establishes a situation and introduces a narrator or characters, uses narrative techniques such as dialogue and description, organizes events in a logical sequence, uses precise words and sensory details, and provides a conclusion that reflects on the experience. Narratives can be fictional or based on real events.

items.prompt: A student wants to write a narrative about getting lost in a shopping mall. They begin: 'One day I went to the mall and got lost and it was scary.' Explain what is weak about this opening and rewrite it using a narrative technique.

steps: Strong narrative openings use a technique to hook the reader: in medias res (starting in the middle of the action), dialogue, sensory description, or a moment of conflict.
The original opening summarizes the entire story in one sentence, removing all tension and surprise.
Identify one technique and rewrite the opening using it.
solution.answer:
The original opening is weak because it tells the reader what happens (got lost, was scary) rather than showing it. It summarizes events instead of immersing the reader in the moment.

Revised opening using sensory description: 'The moment I turned around in the food court, every aisle looked exactly the same: bright fluorescent lights, identical tile floors, and a hundred strangers who all seemed to know exactly where they were going. None of them were my mom.'

items.prompt:
Read this passage from a student narrative and identify what narrative technique is used. Explain how it develops the character.

'"I told you we should have practiced more," Maya said, not looking up from her cleats.
"I know," I said. "I know."
She finally looked at me. Her expression was not angry, which somehow made it worse.
"It's okay. Next time." She picked up her bag and walked toward the bus without looking back.'

steps: Identify the narrative technique: this passage uses dialogue and indirect characterization.
Explain what the dialogue reveals about each character.
Explain how what is NOT said develops character.
solution.answer: The narrative technique used is dialogue with indirect characterization. The dialogue reveals that Maya is disappointed but restrained, choosing to say 'It's okay. Next time' rather than expressing her true feelings. The narrator's repeated 'I know. I know.' suggests guilt and shame. The detail that Maya's non-angry expression 'somehow made it worse' reveals that the narrator expected anger and finds Maya's quiet disappointment harder to bear. The narrator never says they feel guilty, but the reader understands it through the dialogue and specific physical details like Maya not looking up and walking away without looking back.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between showing and telling in narrative writing. Rewrite this sentence using 'showing': 'Marcus was very nervous about his speech.'

steps: 'Telling' states the emotion or fact directly (Marcus was nervous).
'Showing' conveys the emotion through specific physical details, dialogue, or actions that the reader can visualize.
Rewrite by choosing specific physical signals of nervousness.
solution.answer:
Telling states the emotion outright: 'Marcus was very nervous.' Showing reveals the emotion through concrete details so the reader feels it without being told.

Showing version: 'Marcus read the first line of his speech silently one more time, then again. His hands had left damp marks on the index cards. When his name was called, he stood too fast and knocked his chair back with a screech that made the whole class turn to look at him.'

items.prompt:
Read this narrative conclusion and evaluate it.

'And so we finished the hike and went home. It was a great experience. I learned a lot about nature and about myself. It was really fun and I would do it again.'

Explain what is weak about it and describe what a stronger conclusion would include.

steps: A narrative conclusion should reflect on the experience, not just summarize that it ended.
Identify vague or summarizing language in the original.
Describe what the stronger version would show.
solution.answer:
The conclusion is weak because it uses vague language ('great experience,' 'really fun') without showing what specifically was meaningful. 'I learned a lot about nature and about myself' is a claim without any specific insight.

A stronger conclusion would: (1) return to a specific image or moment from earlier in the narrative, creating a sense of closure; (2) show (not tell) the change or insight the narrator experienced; (3) use precise language rather than generic summary phrases.

Example: 'By the time we reached the trailhead, the sun had dropped behind the ridge. I was sweaty, my left knee ached, and I had not thought about the math test for six straight hours. I sat on the wooden post at the trailhead and didn't say anything. For once, I didn't need to.'

items.prompt: A student narrative has this sequence of events: (1) The narrator forgets their lunch. (2) A classmate they don't know well shares their food. (3) They walk home thinking the classmate seems nicer than they thought. What is missing from a well-structured narrative, and how could the student improve the structure?

steps: A well-structured narrative needs: situation setup, rising tension or conflict, a pivotal moment, falling action/reflection, and a conclusion.
Identify what the student's sequence is missing.
Suggest specific additions.
solution.answer:
The sequence is missing several structural elements: (1) An established situation with context, such as who the narrator and classmate are and why they wouldn't normally interact. (2) Tension or internal conflict, such as the narrator's embarrassment about forgetting lunch or hesitation about accepting help. (3) A pivotal moment that feels significant, not just transactional. (4) A meaningful reflection in the conclusion beyond 'they seem nicer.'

Improvement: The student should add internal thoughts showing the narrator's initial reluctance to accept help, dialogue that reveals something unexpected about the classmate, and a conclusion that reflects on why the narrator had misjudged this person.

items.prompt: Write a narrative opening (3-4 sentences) for a story about discovering something unexpected while cleaning out an attic. Use at least one sensory detail and begin in or near the action.
items.hint: Don't start with 'One day...' or 'I was...' Try starting with something the narrator hears, sees, or touches. Make the reader immediately curious.

steps: Choose a sensory detail to anchor the opening (something found, a smell, a sound).
Begin close to the moment of discovery to create immediate tension.
Leave some mystery so the reader wants to keep reading.
solution.answer: Example: 'The box was lighter than it looked. That was the first strange thing. The second was the handwriting on the side, which was mine, except I had never written it. I set the box down on the dusty attic floor and stared at my own eight-year-old cursive spelling out three words: DO NOT OPEN.'

items.prompt: Write a dialogue (4-6 lines) between two characters in a narrative about a misunderstanding. Use the dialogue to show each character's personality without stating it directly.
items.hint: Let what each character says and does NOT say reveal who they are. Include at least one action or gesture alongside the dialogue. Avoid having a character explain themselves too clearly.

steps: Decide on two distinct personalities.
Create a misunderstanding through the dialogue itself.
Add one physical action or gesture to show emotion without telling it.
solution.answer:
Example:
'You said you'd be there,' Dani said.
'I said I'd try.'
'That's the same as saying yes.'
Raj was quiet for a moment. He looked at the floor. 'It really isn't.'
'Well.' Dani picked up her backpack and pulled the straps tight. 'Now we both know that.'

items.prompt: Rewrite this 'telling' sentence as a 'showing' passage of 2-3 sentences: 'Sofia was excited about the first day of school.'
items.hint: Instead of stating 'excited,' describe what excited looks and feels like in the body: what is Sofia doing, thinking, or noticing?

steps: Remove the word 'excited' and any synonyms.
Replace with specific physical actions, thoughts, or observations that convey excitement.
Use at least one concrete sensory detail.
solution.answer: Showing version: 'Sofia had set her backpack by the door the night before. She woke up at 6:14, sixteen minutes before her alarm, and lay in bed staring at the ceiling until she couldn't stand it anymore. The smell of her new colored pencils, even through the pencil case, made her smile.'

items.prompt: Write a narrative conclusion (3-4 sentences) for a story in which a student finally apologizes to a friend after a long argument. The conclusion should reflect on the experience without simply summarizing it.
items.hint: Return to a specific image, object, or detail from the story to create a sense of coming full circle. Show (don't tell) how the narrator feels. The last sentence should leave the reader with something to think about.

steps: Pick a specific image or detail to return to.
Show the narrator's emotional state through action or observation.
End with a line that has some resonance beyond just 'everything is fine now.'
solution.answer: Example: 'We walked home the same route we had taken together every day since fourth grade, past the dog that always barked at us and the mailbox someone had painted orange. Neither of us said much. But when we reached the corner where our streets split, Leah paused. "Same time tomorrow?" "Same time," I said. It wasn't the same as before, but it was something, and something felt like enough.'

items.prompt: Write a complete short narrative (8-10 sentences) about a moment when a character changes their mind about something. Include: a narrative opening, dialogue, at least one 'showing' detail, and a conclusion that reflects on the experience.
items.hint: The change of mind is the pivotal moment of the story. Build to it slowly. Your opening should establish the character's original belief. Your conclusion should show how they see things differently now.

steps: Open with the character holding their original belief.
Build to a scene or conversation that challenges it.
Show the shift through dialogue or action.
Close with a reflection that demonstrates the change.
solution.answer: Example: 'I had decided before the tryouts even started that Diego was trying to take my spot. He was new, he was good, and Coach kept watching him during warm-ups with an expression I had never seen her give anyone else. During the water break, Diego sat next to me, which I had not expected. "You've got a really strong left foot," he said. "I watched your last game on the school's YouTube channel." I didn't know what to say. Nobody had ever said that to me. We ran the last drill together, and he kept feeding me the ball even when he had a clear shot. Walking off the field, I realized I had been so busy worrying about what he was going to take from me that I hadn't noticed what he was trying to give. A season with Diego on the team would be harder in some ways. But looking at the score on the board, I thought it might also be better.'
